en: With a Chinese fire-steel and flint,
Struck sparks and lit a fire.
With rotten saxaul wood,
With dry bones that gave no smoke,
From the cauldron-like lung
She cut portions and cooked them.
To the orphan lying like a lump of stone,
Kanykey gave some.
Tugging it this way and that,
On one side of the lung
Unhappy Chyyyrdy ate her fill.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
The bold woman built like a warrior,
Gave courage to your mother
And stood sobbing and weeping.
“My dear mother,
If my appointed death comes, let me die.
For the orphan left by the Magnanimous One,
Let me try to find some food.
Whoever says, ‘I have only one horse,’
My dear mother,
I will slaughter his horse and eat it.
Whoever says, ‘I myself am alone,’
Mother, I will slaughter him and eat him.
Mother, let me run like a lion;
I, the fierce one, will cast off my weariness
And find some food to bring back.
Until I find food and return,
Mother, until I return and see your face,
Make your way along the foothills.
Noble mother, elder lady,
Grieve for poor me when six days have passed.
If I am gone beyond six days,
Make your preparations for death;
Say, ‘My precious child Kanykey
Has died,’ and go on.
If I am gone beyond seven days,
Mother, braid the hair down your back;
Die before your appointed death.
My dear mother,
Since this has happened to us,
Who might not suffer the same?
Our means are failing us;
The little camel you are soothing
May meet his appointed death today.
Allah the Exalted, the Creator,
May bring turmoil upon our heads.
If I cannot find food by searching,
Your little foal will die of hunger!”
On the black-cheeked battle-axe,
Your leopard sister-in-law leaned.
Without looking all around,
Without sparing her life at all,
Without looking up or down,
Without sparing her mortal life,
“Let me find one beast,” she said.
Without the slightest pity for her poor life,
Her knees bending to the ground,
She ran, offering supplications.
As she ran, she sped like a mirage;
Both her heels
Clapped against her fleshy buttocks.
That accomplished, fierce woman—
The wind could not catch her running.
Yet though she ran, she found no food.
Your poor, fierce sister-in-law
Came upon nothing lawful to eat.
To the foothills of Uch-Koshoy
She ran like a hunting hound.
To the foothills where horses lay,
She came once more.
Again, nothing could be found;
Nothing lawful came her way.
The wide world had grown narrow.
Your sister-in-law grieved and wept,
Yearning for a miracle.
Her heart was utterly distracted;
All her tears had poured away.
Dust filled her mouth;
Your saintly sister-in-law's strength failed.
The bereaved woman who would not eat rich horse-belly meat
Yearned only for a miracle.
Searching for food and finding none,
Your sister-in-law wept in the plain, humiliated.
Running, racing, speeding along,
From her golden-heeled boots
She pulled the heels and threw them away.
To the broken, mottled northern slopes,
To Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
To the ridge of broad Talas,
Along the great Keng-Kol,
Your sister-in-law came.
When she looked, nothing met her eyes.
There was no crow to caw,
There was no raven to croak,
Nor could she tell where anything was.
Offering supplications and sobbing,
Your fleet-steed mother Kanykey
Stood weeping and crying aloud:
“O God, was this a moonless night?
After the Magnanimous One's eyes closed forever,
Unable to find food in the plain,
Was this the day to die like this?
My hero, my prince, if only you had not died!
If only the fierce woman had not suffered such torment!
If only God had not taken the Magnanimous One!
If only no orphan had been left behind!
While the sultan was alive and well,
Was misery what I held in my hands?
When the hero's eyes closed forever,
Was this the road I was to walk?
Unable to find food in the plain,
O God, was this the pit I was to fall into?
Have you dug my pit, God?
Unable to find food in the plain,
O God, have you truly
Made my misery seethe?
Into my mouth that would not hold a grain of wheat,
O God, a bull's head now fits.
Into my mouth that would not hold a grain of millet,
O God, a young ox's head now fits.
Poor soul who would not draw the roof-cover,
I have been humiliated in the plain at night.
You gave me hardship in my youth;
A wretched soul who has suffered misery,
You gave me hardship for my arrogance.
I have no tea to drink for nourishment.
For my orphan and my mother,
I have no colt to load and lead away.
My mother and my orphan—
Nor, poor soul,
Have I the strength to carry them away.
My poor tongue can still speak;
A dark day has fallen upon me.
Oh, leopard, if only you had not died!
Such humiliation as this,
God, if you created us as living souls,
Do not inflict it upon a Muslim!
Deceitful world, may you come to ruin!
May the poor soul suffer no torment!
It seems the bone of my brow slopes backward;
I, unfortunate, steeped in grief,
Have scant prospect of living at all.
My journey is the road to Bukhara.
My good days have left me;
It seems I have no life ahead at all.
Do not take my strength away, God;
Do not torment my soul.
Even if there is no food on this road,
Let me shed my blood like this;
Take my life without tormenting it.
You have shrunk my nights to a handbreadth;
You have used up all my days.
Have you driven away, O God,
My one precious protector?
You named him Khan Manas;
What shall I do about your sultan?
You made him a lion who slew unbelievers.
After the lion's eyes closed forever,
Why, God, have you thus
Made me level with the black earth?
The gray-maned khan of all peoples,
You made him a lion who slew the Chinese.
Making me struggle in search of food,
O God, why have you reduced me so low?
Khojosan, who protected my Bloodstained One,
Look upon the widow!
Who followed twelve spiritual masters,
Lion who has gone to the other world,
Protect your orphan.
Your spring flowing through the valley,
Your little one has now lost all strength.
A host of saints came together;
He was conceived through their prayers.
The day has come to die without eating his fill.
All the saints came together;
He was conceived through their blessings.
When Koshoy gave his blessing,
They gave their blessings with him.
Unbeliever and Muslim
Gave their blessings together.
My little soul conceived through blessings,
Gray-maned khan gone to the other world,
Look upon the orphan!
Host of saints and holy elders,
Give the orphan your protection!
My strength has failed from being beaten.
O God, I stand here bereft.
Hailstones have fallen upon my head;
O God, I stand here wasted away.
Scarcely any blood remains in my body;
No strength remains when I try to walk.
There is no forest to flee into;
No Nogai to give us support,
I have no ridge to put my trust in;
I have no sheltered place.
Finding no cliff that a goose cannot circle,
Finding no inaccessible dark mountain,
I stand here in grief!”
Thus your sister-in-law wept,
Her heart terribly distraught,
Tears pouring from her eyes,
Her limbs giving way as she sobbed.
Turning, weeping and crying aloud,
To Uch-Koshoy's Chatkal
Your sister-in-law came running.
Karymbay's brown calf, nursed by a cow that had not calved again,
A calf fostered by two mothers,
Had been driven away by gadflies
And left at the deserted camp.
“Look at my tears, God;
Give me the brown calf, God!”
May that calf tumble down!
When it saw Kanykey,
It fled downhill, slipping and sliding.
When it saw Kanykey,
May that calf tumble down!
It fled uphill in a frenzy.
Then your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
Her wide world grown narrow,
Longing for the brown calf,
Could not catch it in pursuit.
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Tears fell drop after drop.
From her dear currant-like eyes,
Tears ran a whip's length.
Kanykey pondered a plan:
“If I could catch and slaughter the calf,
If I could feed my orphan just once!”
May that calf tumble down!
It scampered about the mountain.
Your tormented sister-in-law Kanykey
Pursued it, crying aloud.
Karymbay's calf
Scampered along the ridge.
Struggling to chase the calf,
Hard pressed and unable to catch it,
Your sister-in-law went on sobbing and weeping.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
Around the lower slopes of Uch-Koshoy,
Chased it three times;
Around the sweep of Beles-Tash,
Chased it five times.
Your heroic sister-in-law Kanykey
Stood gathering courage.
“The fate God has imposed
Is like this; let me face it.
Rather than groan and starve in the plain,
Rather than endure this humiliation,
Let me die chasing the calf.
O God, if I could chase it down and slaughter it,
My mother who has grown old,
At least, oh world,
I could give her some relief.”
Around Uyurulmo's Chatkal
She chased it three times.
